title: The Craft and Malice of Woman

full_text:
A wise king of ancient Persia had an only son whom he had placed under the tutelage of the renowned sage Sindibad. The prince grew up in mastery of sciences, horsemanship, and statecraft.

However, an astrological prophecy warned that if the prince spoke a single word during seven consecutive days, his life would be forfeited. The prince accordingly observed a strict vow of total silence.

During those seven days, an envious courtier falsely accused the silent prince of treason before the king. The monarch, blinded by sudden wrath, ordered his son to be led to the scaffold!

Before the executioner could strike, the King’s First Vizier stepped forward and said: 'O King, do not act in hasty anger! He who judges without hearing the defense will reap a lifetime of bitter remorse, even as the king who destroyed his faithful falcon!'

The vizier recounted a tale of the perils of hasty wrath, and the king stayed the execution for one day.

On the second day, the accusers renewed their pressure, but the Second Vizier stepped forward, recounting an ancient history of patient inquiry, winning another day of reprieve.

Day after day, for seven consecutive days, the Seven Wise Viziers matched their philosophical parables against the fires of hasty anger, shielding the silent prince with shields of narrative wisdom.

On the eighth day, the period of the prophecy expired. The prince broke his silence, stepped boldly before the throne, and delivered an eloquent defense supported by documented evidence that exposed the false conspiracy!

The king embraced his son with tears of joy, honored the Seven Viziers for their courageous intervention, and learned that patient counsel is the truest guardian of the throne.
moral: Hasty execution without impartial inquiry is the ruin of kings; patient counsel preserves justice.
